summary: Sam Denton introduces a two-axis framework for continual learning in enterprises. The first axis is the online-ness of traces: from a one-time batch of production traces, through daily batches, to a unified engine where serving and training form one loop (the "holy grail"). The second axis is the source of the hint used to construct a teacher smarter than the on-policy student: offline hints derived from static priors (e.g., a support agent too quick to refund) versus online hints dynamically constructed from the rollout the on-policy model just produced. This yields four quadrants. Quadrant one pairs offline hints with offline traces and lets Applied Compute improve an agent from a data dump on day one, with no replayable environment. Quadrant four pairs online hints with online traces and represents the full flywheel: a model serving production traffic, constructing hints from its own rollout, and updating continuously. Denton notes they work across all four but focus on quadrants one and four. He stresses the constraint that none of this assumes a golden answer to distill toward, which he sees as a common and unrealistic assumption in the distillation literature. On SWE-bench, they targeted a Qwen thinking model taking up to 80 turns to submit, with the goal of submission before turn 40. Three metrics were tracked: complete rate (percentage of times the agent calls the submit tool), test pass rate (whether the environment passes all tests irrespective of submission), and SWE-bench pass rate (the intersection of the two). The hint text told the model it was near its 40-turn limit and should finalize, verify, and call the tool. Results: the submit tool call rate rose from about 22% to 60% with test pass rate holding flat or slightly improving. The surprising mechanism was that because the rollout was conditioned on a production trace that never called the tool, the teacher never touched the tool-call tokens; instead it moved the reasoning path toward the call, and the call followed. Adding a single on-policy step from the offline trace improved the SWE-bench pass rate further. For a customer requiring unusual hyperlink formatting, both direct rewards and SFT on correct examples degraded coding ability, but an online hint written against each rollout took correct formatting from about 15% to 80%. Two practical techniques make this work: per-step hinting, where a judge picks where in the rollout the hint goes and distillation covers only the next few steps because the KL learning signal decays with distance from the hint; and relevance-masked self-distillation, where an LLM judge selects which teacher tokens to learn from, filtering out the teacher's preferences on irrelevant connector words and avoiding catastrophic degradation.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Continual learning can be framed on two axes: online-ness of traces and source of the hint.
Offline hints on offline traces let enterprises improve agents from a one-time data dump with no replayable environment.
Online hints on online traces form the full flywheel where serving and training are one loop, offering the highest ceiling.
All approaches are designed to work without a golden answer to distill toward.

For hyperlink formatting, rewards and SFT both degraded coding ability, but per-rollout online hints took correct formatting from 15% to 80%.
Per-step hinting—letting a judge choose hint placement and distilling only the next few steps—preserves signal because learning decays with distance from the hint.

sections.title: Introduction and agenda
sections.summary: Sam Denton introduces himself as lead of the platform research team at Applied Compute and outlines the agenda: distillation spectrum, where value accrues, enterprise data, tips and tricks, and lessons learned.

sections.title: The distillation spectrum, offline to online
sections.summary: Defines the offline-to-online distillation spectrum: from a single batch of production traces, to daily batches, to a unified engine where inference and training are one loop serving production traffic.

sections.title: Where enterprises sit and meeting them where they are
sections.summary: Most enterprises are on the offline end with production dumps; some are ready for fully online continual learning. Applied Compute aims to provide value across both ends.

sections.title: Where the hint comes from
sections.summary: Introduces the second axis: hint source. Offline hints come from static data such as rubrics or behavior priors. Online hints are dynamically constructed from the on-policy rollout.

sections.title: Four quadrants of distillation
sections.summary: Describes the four quadrants: offline hint + offline trace; offline hint + on-policy online trace; off-policy trace with one on-policy step and hint built from that step; online hint + online trace. Applied Compute focuses on quadrants one and four.

sections.title: Improve for free today, raise ceilings tomorrow
sections.summary: Maps the grid to value: offline traces let enterprises improve for free from a data dump; online traces raise ceilings continuously. Emphasizes doing this without golden answers.

sections.title: SWE-bench setup and metrics
sections.summary: Introduces the SWE-bench experiment: a Qwen thinking model taking up to 80 turns to submit, with a goal of submitting before turn 40, and previews three metrics to evaluate the approach.

sections.title: SWE-bench hint text and results
sections.summary: Defines the three metrics—complete rate, test pass rate, and SWE-bench pass rate (their intersection). The hint text tells the model it is near its 40-turn limit and should finalize, verify, and call the submit tool. Submit tool call rate rose from about 22% to 60% with test pass rate flat or slightly up.

sections.title: Mechanism: moving the reasoning path, not the tool call
sections.summary: The surprising result: because the rollout was conditioned on a production trace that never called the tool, the teacher never changed the tool-call tokens. Instead it moved the reasoning path toward the call, and the call followed. Adding one on-policy step from the offline trace improved the SWE-bench pass rate further.

sections.title: The hyperlink formatting problem
sections.summary: A customer's coding agent needed very specific out-of-distribution hyperlink formatting. Direct rewards and SFT on correct examples both degraded coding ability. Online hints—per-rollout messages correcting the formatting—raised correct formatting from about 15% to 80%, far outperforming offline hinting.

sections.title: Per-step hinting and signal decay
sections.summary: Per-step hinting is critical: a judge decides where in the rollout to inject the hint, and distillation covers only the next few steps. The KL learning signal decays with distance from the hint, making late-rollout distillation less useful.

sections.title: Relevance masked self-distillation
sections.summary: An LLM judge selects which teacher tokens to learn from, filtering out the teacher's preferences on irrelevant connector words. This increases the ability to learn out-of-distribution behaviors while avoiding catastrophic degradation.

sections.title: Conclusion and hiring
sections.summary: Recaps the two-axis framework and the two corners they work in: offline hints on offline traces for day-one value, and online hints on online traces for continuous improvement. Thanks the team and invites interest in hiring.
